newsitem.title: USA: Indianapolis taps revenues for airport facility.
newsitem.headline: Indianapolis taps revenues for airport facility.

text.p: Three years after expressing concern over finding the necessary revenues to pay off $140 million of lease revenue bonds for an United Airlines maintenance facility, Indianapolis Mayor Stephen Goldsmith has laid out a funding plan that taps the city's surplus and creates a tax increment financing district.

At a news conference Sunday in Indianapolis, Goldsmith proposed using $6 million annually from the city's budget surplus and another $4.2 million annually from a new TIF district around a recently privatized Naval Air Warfare Center, a former government installation to pay off the debt.

A news release from the mayor's office said the city has paid off $30 million of the debt, leaving $188 million. A city finance official said that amount represents principal and interest on the $140 million of bonds.
Goldsmith said that competition through his privatization efforts of city services has increased Indianapolis' budget surplus to more than $100 million this year from $24 million in 1992.
He proposed maintaining the budget surplus at around $89 million, using the remaining revenue to pay off the maintenance facility bonds.

The city had pledged revenues from its county option income tax to pay off $140 million of lease revenue bonds sold through the Indianapolis Local Public Improvement Bond Bank in 1991 to fund the city's share of the more than $1 billion United Airlines project. The bonds are rated A1 by Moody's Investors Service.

Goldsmith in 1994 said that most of the income tax revenues were slated for the city's police and fire budgets and city finance officials said the search was on to identify new revenues for debt service.

Under the proposed plan unveiled Sunday, surplus budget money would also be used to pay for $55 million of targeted improvements to the city's combined sewer overflow system in order to comply with environmental regulations, Goldsmith said.

The mayor also announced the city's obligation to police and fire pension funds through 2000 has been reduced to about $8 million from around $55 million due to prudent management, revised financial forecasts and action by the Indiana General Assembly.
Goldsmith said the obligation would be paid off with a combination of existing revenues, including property taxes and the county option income tax.

A fourth element of the plan, which the mayor plans to present to the city-county council Monday evening, calls for a reduction in the property tax rate to $3.79 per $100 assessed valuation from $3.80.
